title: Diffusion Processes
text:
I suggest the reader not accustomed to the language of probability to first read an introductory measure theory set of lecture notes. The following is not an easy read, but it contains all the necessary definitions and results we will need throughout the course.


Recall that a \(\sigma\)-algebra represents available information.
In a dynamical setting, information changes with time. We therefore consider a family of \(\sigma\)-algebras
\[
\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq 0}.
\]
A filtration is an increasing family of sub-\(\sigma\)-algebras of \(\mathcal{F}\):
\[
\mathcal{F}_s
\subseteq
\mathcal{F}_t
\subseteq
\mathcal{F},
\qquad
s\leq t.
\]
Hence \(\mathcal{F}_t\) contains all information available up to time \(t\). Imagine yourself reading a book: the information you have at time \(t\) is the information contained in the first \(t\) pages, and your information set is increasing as you read more pages.


Given a stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t\geq0}\), its natural filtration is
\[
\mathcal{F}_t^X
=
\sigma(X_s:0\leq s\leq t).
\]
It is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra that makes all observations
\[
X_s,
\qquad s\leq t,
\]
measurable. I like to think of this as the least information that should be contained in the first \(t\) pages of a book in order to understand the story up to that point.




A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}\) is adapted to a filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) if
\[
X_t
\quad\text{is }\mathcal{F}_t\text{-measurable}
\]
for every \(t\).
Informally, the value \(X_t\) can be determined using information available at time \(t\).
An adapted process therefore cannot depend on future information.
Every process is automatically adapted to its own natural filtration:
\[
X_t
\text{ is }
\mathcal{F}_t^X\text{-measurable}.
\]
To end the book analogy, in our book we are able to understand the story up to page \(t\) without having to peek ahead.




Informally, a Markov process is a stochastic process that retains no memory.
We now set
\[
\mathcal F_t^X:=\sigma\{X_s:s\leq t\}.
\]
Then a process \(\{X_t,\ t\in\mathbb R_+\}\) is a Markov process if
\[
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid\mathcal F_s^X)
=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_s),
\qquad t\geq s.
\]
which is, the history of the process up to time \(s\) is irrelevant for predicting the future at time \(t\). Only the present matters.


Define the transition function
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
:=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_s=x).
\]
It is a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\) and satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(\Gamma,t\mid y,u)\,
P(dy,u\mid x,s),
\]
where \(\Gamma\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\), \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(s\leq u\leq t\).
This formula merely states that the probability of going from \(x\) at time \(s\) to \(\Gamma\) at time \(t\) is the sum of the probabilities of going from \(x\) at time \(s\) to \(y\) at time \(u\), and then from \(y\) at time \(u\) to \(\Gamma\) at time \(t\), integrated over all possible intermediate states \(y\). Iterating the argument can be useful to see why it works. The proof can also be useful:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
&=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_s=x)\\
&=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid\mathcal F_s^X)\\
&=
\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)\mid\mathcal F_s^X]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb E[
        \mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)
        \mid\mathcal F_s^X
    ]
    \mid\mathcal F_u^X
\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb E[
        \mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)
        \mid\mathcal F_u^X
    ]
    \mid\mathcal F_s^X
\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb E[
        \mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)
        \mid X_u
    ]
    \mid\mathcal F_s^X
\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_u=y)
    \mid X_s=x
\right]\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(\Gamma,t\mid y,u)\,
P(dy,u\mid x,s).
\end{aligned}
\]



Now rewrite the transition function as
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_\Gamma
p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy,
\]
where \(p(\cdot\mid\cdot)\) is the transition probability density.
Chapman–Kolmogorov becomes
\[
\int_\Gamma p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(\Gamma,t\mid z,u)
P(dz,u\mid x,s),
\]
hence
\[
\int_\Gamma p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\int_\Gamma
p(y,t\mid z,u)
p(z,u\mid x,s)
\,dy\,dz.
\]
It follows that
\[
p(y,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
p(y,t\mid z,u)
p(z,u\mid x,s)
\,dz.
\]
as before.
Consider now a time-homogeneous Markov process,
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
=
P(\Gamma,t-s\mid x,0)
=:P(t-s,x,\Gamma).
\]
Then
\[
P(t+s,x,\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(t,z,\Gamma)\,
P(s,x,dz).
\]
Or, in terms of the transition density,
\[
p(t+s,x,y)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
p(t,z,y)
p(s,x,z)\,dz.
\]
Which makes sense if we think of restarting the clock at every intermediate step.
Notice that the transition function and the initial distribution are sufficient to determine the law of a Markov process.
If the process starts from an arbitrary point \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), its initial distribution is the Dirac delta
\[
\nu(dx)=\delta_{x_0}(dx),
\]
where \(\delta_{x_0}\) is the probability measure concentrated at \(x_0\), defined by
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x)\,\delta_{x_0}(dx)=f(x_0).
\]
Hence,
\[
\mathbb P_{x_0}(X_t\in\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(x,t,\Gamma)\,\delta_{x_0}(dx)
=
P(x_0,t,\Gamma).
\]
More generally, if the initial condition is distributed according to \(\nu\),
\[
\mathbb P_\nu(X_t\in\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(x,t,\Gamma)\,\nu(dx).
\]
So the general formula simply averages the transition probabilities over all possible starting points.
Similarly, we can calculate the expectation for an observable \(f\):
\[
\mathbb E_\nu[f(X_t)]
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(x)
\underbrace{
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\nu(dx_0)\,
P(x_0,t,dx)
}_{\mu_t(dx)}.
\]




To describe time-homogeneous Markov processes, introduce a single-parameter family of linear operators such that
\[
P_0=I,
\]
and
\[
P_{t+s}=P_tP_s,
\qquad
\forall s,t\geq0.
\]
Define
\[
P_t f(x)
:=
\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_0=x]
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)P(t,x,dy).
\]
As expected,
\[
P_0f(x)
=
\mathbb E[f(X_0)\mid X_0=x]
=
f(x).
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{t+s}f(x)
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)P(t+s,x,dy)\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)
P(t,z,dy)
P(s,x,dz)\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P_tf(z)
P(s,x,dz)\\
&=
P_s\circ P_tf(x).
\end{aligned}
\]


Now define \(D(\mathcal L)\) as the set of all \(f\in C_b(E)\) such that
\[
\mathcal Lf
:=
\lim_{t\to0}
\frac{P_tf-f}{t}
\]
exists.
Then the operator \(\mathcal L\) is the infinitesimal generator of \(P_t\), or the generator of the Markov process.
Now,
\[
\mathcal L
=
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{P_h-I}{h},
\]
which reminds us of the definition of the derivative. Notice:
\[
P_h\approx I+h\mathcal L.
\]
Then
\[
P_t
=
\left(P_{t/n}\right)^n
\approx
\left(
I+\frac{t}{n}\mathcal L
\right)^n.
\]
(verify the first equality using the semigroup property). Taking the limit,
\[
P_t
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\left(
I+\frac{t}{n}\mathcal L
\right)^n
=
e^{t\mathcal L}.
\]
Now define
\[
u(x,t):=P_tf(x)
\]
and say we want to find the equation governing \(P_t\), i.e. determining the evolution of the conditional expectation of the observable \(f\).
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}u(x,t)
&=
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{
P_{t+h}f(x)-P_tf(x)
}{h}\\
&=
P_t\mathcal Lf(x)\\
&=
\mathcal L P_tf(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal Lu.
\]
Since \(P_0=I\), we have
\[
u(x,0)=f(x).
\]
Hence \(u(x,t)\) satisfies the initial value problem
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal Lu,\\[6pt]
u(x,0)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
This is the backward Kolmogorov equation.




While \(P_t\) acts on continuous bounded functions, we can define \(P_t^*\), which acts on probability measures:
\[
P_t^*\mu(\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(t,x,\Gamma)\,d\mu(x).
\]
Formally, we have
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P_tf(x)\,d\mu(x)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(x)\,d(P_t^*\mu)(x).
\]
Which makes sense if we think of \(P_t^*\) as the \(L^2\) adjoint of \(P_t\). We can also define, as before, the generator \(\mathcal L^*\) of the semigroup \(P_t^*\), and we have
\[
P_t^*
=
e^{t\mathcal L^*}.
\]
Also,
\[
\int
(\mathcal Lf)\,d\mu
=
\int
f(\mathcal L^*\mu)\,dx.
\]
Now define the law of the Markov process as
\[
\mu_t
=
P_t^*\mu,
\]
which evolves according to
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial\mu_t}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal L^*\mu_t,\\[6pt]
\mu_0=\mu.
\end{cases}
\]
Assuming \(\mu\) and \(\mu_t\) have densities, denote them by \(\rho_0(\cdot)\) and \(\rho(\cdot,t)\).
Then
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal L^*\rho,\\[6pt]
\rho(x,0)=\rho_0(x).
\end{cases}
\]
Is the Fokker–Planck, or forward Kolmogorov, equation.
To conclude this introduction, the backward and forward Kolmogorov equations describe the evolution of the same Markov process from two complementary perspectives.
The backward Kolmogorov equation governs the evolution of an observable \(f\), as it tells us how the expected future value of \(f(X_t)\) depends on the initial state \(x\):
\[
\partial_t u=\mathcal L u.
\]
The forward Kolmogorov equation, instead, governs the evolution of the law of the process. If \(\rho(x,t)\) is the probability density of \(X_t\), then
\[
\partial_t\rho=\mathcal L^*\rho.
\]
Hence, \(\mathcal L\) propagates observables, while its adjoint \(\mathcal L^*\) propagates probability distributions.



A Markov process consists of three parts:

a drift;
a random part;
a jump process.

A diffusion process is a Markov process with continuous paths, hence no jumps.
In one dimension, we need the following.


For all \(\varepsilon>0\) and all \(x\),
\[
\int_{|x-y|>\varepsilon}
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
o(t-s).
\]



There exists \(b(x,s)\) such that, for all \(\varepsilon>0\) and all \(x\),
\[
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
(y-x)
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
b(x,s)(t-s)
+
o(t-s).
\]



There exists \(\Sigma(x,s)\) such that, for all \(\varepsilon>0\) and all \(x\),
\[
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
(y-x)^2
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
\Sigma(x,s)(t-s)
+
o(t-s).
\]
Assuming that the first two moments exist, we can write, even more intuitively,
\[
b(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\mathbb E
\left[
\frac{X_t-X_s}{t-s}
\mid X_s=x
\right],
\]
and
\[
\Sigma(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\mathbb E
\left[
\frac{(X_t-X_s)^2}{t-s}
\mid X_s=x
\right].
\]




From the definition of a diffusion process, we can derive explicit formulas for the forward and backward Kolmogorov equations.


Let
\[
u(x,s)
:=
\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s=x]
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s).
\]
Then \(u(x,s)\) solves the final value problem for a PDE of parabolic type:
\[
\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial s}
=
b(x,s)
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s)
\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2},
\\[8pt]
u(x,t)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
Parts of the proof are very interesting, so I recommend reading it at least once.
Proof:
The continuity assumption for the diffusion process, together with the boundedness of \(f\), implies that
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x,s)
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&\leq
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
\lVert f\rVert_{L^\infty}
\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
o(t-s).
\end{aligned}
\]
We add and subtract the final condition \(f(x)\) and use the previous calculation to obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x,s)
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
f(x)
+
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
f(x)
+
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&\qquad
+
\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
f(x)
+
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
o(t-s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Now we show that \(u(s,x)\) solves the backward Kolmogorov equation. We use the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x,\sigma)
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
f(z)P(dz,t\mid x,\sigma)
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
f(z)P(dz,t\mid y,\rho)
P(dy,\rho\mid x,\sigma)
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
u(y,\rho)P(dy,\rho\mid x,\sigma).
\end{aligned}
\]
Where we are integrating over future paths. We use Taylor’s theorem to obtain
\[
u(z,\rho)-u(x,\rho)
=
\frac{\partial u(x,\rho)}{\partial x}(z-x)
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{\partial^2u(x,\rho)}{\partial x^2}
(z-x)^2(1+\alpha_\varepsilon),
\qquad |z-x|\leq\varepsilon,
\]
where
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\alpha_\varepsilon=0.
\]
Now we will use the last two results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{u(x,s)-u(x,s+h)}{h}
&=
\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)u(y,s+h)
-
u(x,s+h)
\right)
\\
&=
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
\bigl(u(y,s+h)-u(x,s+h)\bigr)
\\
&=
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{|x-y|<\varepsilon}
P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
\bigl(u(y,s+h)-u(x,s+h)\bigr)
+
o(1)
\\
&=
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x,s+h)
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{|x-y|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
\\
&\qquad
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}(x,s+h)
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{|x-y|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)^2P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
(1+\alpha_\varepsilon)
+
o(1)
\\
&=
b(x,s)
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x,s+h)
+
\frac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s)
\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}(x,s+h)
(1+\alpha_\varepsilon)
+
o(1).
\end{aligned}
\]
where we have used the definition of the drift and diffusion coefficients in the last step. The result follows by taking the limit \(h\to0\) and \(\varepsilon\to0\).
If \(b=b(x)\) and \(\Sigma=\Sigma(x)\), we can rewrite this as an initial value problem by letting
\[
v=u(x,t-s).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial(t-s)}
=
b(x)\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x)
\dfrac{\partial^2v}{\partial x^2},
\\[8pt]
v(x,0)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
In the time-homogeneous case, we can finally set \(s=0\) to write
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
b(x)\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x)
\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2},
\\[8pt]
u(x,0)=f(x),
\end{cases}
\]
where
\[
\mathcal L
=
b(x)\partial_x
+
\frac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x)\partial_{xx}.
\]



We have
\[
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy.
\]
Under suitable conditions, the transition probability density is the solution to the initial value problem
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial t}
=
-\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}
\left(
b(t,y)p
\right)
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\dfrac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2}
\left(
\Sigma(t,y)p
\right),
\\[10pt]
p(y,s\mid x,s)
=
\delta(x-y).
\end{cases}
\]
The proof is less interesting than the backward case, but it is presented for completeness.
Proof:
Fix \(f(y)\in C_0^2(\mathbb{R})\). An argument similar to that used in the proof of the backward Kolmogorov equation gives
\[
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)p(y,s+h\mid x,s)\,dy-f(x)
\right)
=
b(x,s)\frac{df}{dx}(x)
+
\frac{1}{2}\Sigma(x,s)\frac{d^2f}{dx^2}(x).
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
f(y)\frac{\partial}{\partial t}p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(y)p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
\\
&=
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{1}{h}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\bigl(p(y,t+h\mid x,s)-p(y,t\mid x,s)\bigr)f(y)\,dy
\\
&=
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}}p(y,t+h\mid x,s)f(y)\,dy
-
\int_{\mathbb{R}}p(z,t\mid x,s)f(z)\,dz
\right)
\\
&=
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}
p(y,t+h\mid z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)f(y)\,dy\,dz
-
\int_{\mathbb{R}}p(z,t\mid x,s)f(z)\,dz
\right)
\\
&=
\lim_{h\to0}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
p(z,t\mid x,s)
\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}}p(y,t+h\mid z,t)f(y)\,dy-f(z)
\right)dz
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
p(z,t\mid x,s)
\left(
b(z,t)\frac{df}{dz}(z)
+
\frac{1}{2}\Sigma(z,t)\frac{d^2f}{dz^2}(z)
\right)dz
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
b(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)f'(z)\,dz
+
\frac{1}{2}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\Sigma(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)f''(z)\,dz
\\
&=
\left[
b(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)f(z)
\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}
-
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\bigl(b(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)f(z)\,dz
\\
&\quad
+
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\Sigma(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)f'(z)
\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}
-
\frac{1}{2}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\bigl(\Sigma(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)f'(z)\,dz
\\
&=
-
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\bigl(b(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)f(z)\,dz
\\
&\quad
-
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\bigl(\Sigma(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)f(z)
\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\\
&\quad
+
\frac{1}{2}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}
\bigl(\Sigma(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)f(z)\,dz
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\left(
-
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}
\bigl(b(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}
\bigl(\Sigma(z,t)p(z,t\mid x,s)\bigr)
\right)f(z)\,dz.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the boundary terms vanish since \(f\in C_0^2(\mathbb{R})\). Hence
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\left[
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}
+
\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(bp)
-
\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(\Sigma p)
\right]f(z)\,dz
=0
\]
for every \(f\in C_0^2(\mathbb{R})\). Therefore the integrand is zero (in the weak sense, and pointwise under the assumed smoothness), giving
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}
=
-\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(bp)
+
\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(\Sigma p).
}
\]
Assume that the initial distribution of \(X_t\) is \(\rho_0(x)\) and set \(s=0\) above.
Define
\[
\rho(y,t)
:=
\int
p(y,t\mid x,0)
\rho_0(x)\,dx.
\]
Then we can obtain the probability density at y of the process \(X_t\), initially distributed according to \(\rho_0(x)\).
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}
=
-\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}
\left(
b \rho
\right)
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\dfrac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2}
\left(
\Sigma \rho
\right),
\\[10pt]
\rho(y,0)=\rho_0(y).
\end{cases}
\]




For a process in \(\mathbb R^d\), we define the drift and diffusion coefficients
\[
b(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\frac{1}{t-s}
\int_{|y-x|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)
P(dy,t\mid x,s),
\]
and
\[
\Sigma(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\frac{1}{t-s}
\int_{|y-x|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)\otimes(y-x)
P(dy,t\mid x,s).
\]
As before, the generator is
\[
\mathcal L
=
b(x,s)\cdot\nabla
+
\frac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s):\nabla\nabla,
\]
where
\[
A:\nabla\nabla f
=
\sum_{i,j}
A_{ij}
\frac{\partial^2f}
{\partial x_i\partial x_j}.
\]


The backward Kolmogorov equation is
\[
\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial s}
=
b(x,s)\cdot\nabla_xu
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s):\nabla_x\nabla_xu,
\\[10pt]
u(t,x)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
For a time-homogeneous process, this becomes
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal Lu,
\\[6pt]
u(x,0)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]



The forward Kolmogorov equation is
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial t}
=
\nabla_y\cdot
\left(
-b(t,y)p
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\nabla_y\cdot
\left(
\Sigma(t,y)p
\right)
\right),
\\[10pt]
p(y,s\mid x,s)
=
\delta(x-y).
\end{cases}
\]
For a time-homogeneous process,
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal L^*\rho,
\\[6pt]
\rho(x,0)=\rho_0(x).
\end{cases}
\]

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
Recall that a \(\sigma\)-algebra represents available information.
In a dynamical setting, information changes with time. We therefore consider a family of \(\sigma\)-algebras
\[
\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq 0}.
\]
A filtration is an increasing family of sub-\(\sigma\)-algebras of \(\mathcal{F}\):
\[
\mathcal{F}_s
\subseteq
\mathcal{F}_t
\subseteq
\mathcal{F},
\qquad
s\leq t.
\]
Hence \(\mathcal{F}_t\) contains all information available up to time \(t\). Imagine yourself reading a book: the information you have at time \(t\) is the information contained in the first \(t\) pages, and your information set is increasing as you read more pages.


Given a stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t\geq0}\), its natural filtration is
\[
\mathcal{F}_t^X
=
\sigma(X_s:0\leq s\leq t).
\]
It is the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra that makes all observations
\[
X_s,
\qquad s\leq t,
\]
measurable. I like to think of this as the least information that should be contained in the first \(t\) pages of a book in order to understand the story up to that point.




A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}\) is adapted to a filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\) if
\[
X_t
\quad\text{is }\mathcal{F}_t\text{-measurable}
\]
for every \(t\).
Informally, the value \(X_t\) can be determined using information available at time \(t\).
An adapted process therefore cannot depend on future information.
Every process is automatically adapted to its own natural filtration:
\[
X_t
\text{ is }
\mathcal{F}_t^X\text{-measurable}.
\]
To end the book analogy, in our book we are able to understand the story up to page \(t\) without having to peek ahead.

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
A stochastic process is a family of random variables
\[
X=\{X_t\}_{t\in T}
\]
defined on the same probability space
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}),
\]
with values in some state space \(E\).
Usually,
\[
T=[0,\infty)
\]
and
\[
E=\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
The process can equivalently be viewed as a function of two variables,
\[
X:T\times\Omega\to E,
\]
with
\[
X(t,\omega)=X_t(\omega).
\]
There are two complementary ways to look at it.
For fixed \(t\),
\[
\omega\mapsto X_t(\omega)
\]
is a random variable.
For fixed \(\omega\),
\[
t\mapsto X_t(\omega)
\]
is a function of time, called a sample path, trajectory, or realization of the process.

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
Informally, a Markov process is a stochastic process that retains no memory.
We now set
\[
\mathcal F_t^X:=\sigma\{X_s:s\leq t\}.
\]
Then a process \(\{X_t,\ t\in\mathbb R_+\}\) is a Markov process if
\[
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid\mathcal F_s^X)
=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_s),
\qquad t\geq s.
\]
which is, the history of the process up to time \(s\) is irrelevant for predicting the future at time \(t\). Only the present matters.


Define the transition function
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
:=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_s=x).
\]
It is a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\) and satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(\Gamma,t\mid y,u)\,
P(dy,u\mid x,s),
\]
where \(\Gamma\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\), \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(s\leq u\leq t\).
This formula merely states that the probability of going from \(x\) at time \(s\) to \(\Gamma\) at time \(t\) is the sum of the probabilities of going from \(x\) at time \(s\) to \(y\) at time \(u\), and then from \(y\) at time \(u\) to \(\Gamma\) at time \(t\), integrated over all possible intermediate states \(y\). Iterating the argument can be useful to see why it works. The proof can also be useful:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
&=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_s=x)\\
&=
\mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid\mathcal F_s^X)\\
&=
\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)\mid\mathcal F_s^X]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb E[
        \mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)
        \mid\mathcal F_s^X
    ]
    \mid\mathcal F_u^X
\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb E[
        \mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)
        \mid\mathcal F_u^X
    ]
    \mid\mathcal F_s^X
\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb E[
        \mathbf 1_\Gamma(X_t)
        \mid X_u
    ]
    \mid\mathcal F_s^X
\right]\\
&=
\mathbb E\left[
    \mathbb P(X_t\in\Gamma\mid X_u=y)
    \mid X_s=x
\right]\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(\Gamma,t\mid y,u)\,
P(dy,u\mid x,s).
\end{aligned}
\]



Now rewrite the transition function as
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_\Gamma
p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy,
\]
where \(p(\cdot\mid\cdot)\) is the transition probability density.
Chapman–Kolmogorov becomes
\[
\int_\Gamma p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(\Gamma,t\mid z,u)
P(dz,u\mid x,s),
\]
hence
\[
\int_\Gamma p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\int_\Gamma
p(y,t\mid z,u)
p(z,u\mid x,s)
\,dy\,dz.
\]
It follows that
\[
p(y,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
p(y,t\mid z,u)
p(z,u\mid x,s)
\,dz.
\]
as before.
Consider now a time-homogeneous Markov process,
\[
P(\Gamma,t\mid x,s)
=
P(\Gamma,t-s\mid x,0)
=:P(t-s,x,\Gamma).
\]
Then
\[
P(t+s,x,\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(t,z,\Gamma)\,
P(s,x,dz).
\]
Or, in terms of the transition density,
\[
p(t+s,x,y)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
p(t,z,y)
p(s,x,z)\,dz.
\]
Which makes sense if we think of restarting the clock at every intermediate step.
Notice that the transition function and the initial distribution are sufficient to determine the law of a Markov process.
If the process starts from an arbitrary point \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\), its initial distribution is the Dirac delta
\[
\nu(dx)=\delta_{x_0}(dx),
\]
where \(\delta_{x_0}\) is the probability measure concentrated at \(x_0\), defined by
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x)\,\delta_{x_0}(dx)=f(x_0).
\]
Hence,
\[
\mathbb P_{x_0}(X_t\in\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(x,t,\Gamma)\,\delta_{x_0}(dx)
=
P(x_0,t,\Gamma).
\]
More generally, if the initial condition is distributed according to \(\nu\),
\[
\mathbb P_\nu(X_t\in\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(x,t,\Gamma)\,\nu(dx).
\]
So the general formula simply averages the transition probabilities over all possible starting points.
Similarly, we can calculate the expectation for an observable \(f\):
\[
\mathbb E_\nu[f(X_t)]
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(x)
\underbrace{
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\nu(dx_0)\,
P(x_0,t,dx)
}_{\mu_t(dx)}.
\]

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
To describe time-homogeneous Markov processes, introduce a single-parameter family of linear operators such that
\[
P_0=I,
\]
and
\[
P_{t+s}=P_tP_s,
\qquad
\forall s,t\geq0.
\]
Define
\[
P_t f(x)
:=
\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_0=x]
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)P(t,x,dy).
\]
As expected,
\[
P_0f(x)
=
\mathbb E[f(X_0)\mid X_0=x]
=
f(x).
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{t+s}f(x)
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)P(t+s,x,dy)\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)
P(t,z,dy)
P(s,x,dz)\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P_tf(z)
P(s,x,dz)\\
&=
P_s\circ P_tf(x).
\end{aligned}
\]


Now define \(D(\mathcal L)\) as the set of all \(f\in C_b(E)\) such that
\[
\mathcal Lf
:=
\lim_{t\to0}
\frac{P_tf-f}{t}
\]
exists.
Then the operator \(\mathcal L\) is the infinitesimal generator of \(P_t\), or the generator of the Markov process.
Now,
\[
\mathcal L
=
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{P_h-I}{h},
\]
which reminds us of the definition of the derivative. Notice:
\[
P_h\approx I+h\mathcal L.
\]
Then
\[
P_t
=
\left(P_{t/n}\right)^n
\approx
\left(
I+\frac{t}{n}\mathcal L
\right)^n.
\]
(verify the first equality using the semigroup property). Taking the limit,
\[
P_t
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\left(
I+\frac{t}{n}\mathcal L
\right)^n
=
e^{t\mathcal L}.
\]
Now define
\[
u(x,t):=P_tf(x)
\]
and say we want to find the equation governing \(P_t\), i.e. determining the evolution of the conditional expectation of the observable \(f\).
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}u(x,t)
&=
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{
P_{t+h}f(x)-P_tf(x)
}{h}\\
&=
P_t\mathcal Lf(x)\\
&=
\mathcal L P_tf(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal Lu.
\]
Since \(P_0=I\), we have
\[
u(x,0)=f(x).
\]
Hence \(u(x,t)\) satisfies the initial value problem
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal Lu,\\[6pt]
u(x,0)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
This is the backward Kolmogorov equation.

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
While \(P_t\) acts on continuous bounded functions, we can define \(P_t^*\), which acts on probability measures:
\[
P_t^*\mu(\Gamma)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P(t,x,\Gamma)\,d\mu(x).
\]
Formally, we have
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
P_tf(x)\,d\mu(x)
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(x)\,d(P_t^*\mu)(x).
\]
Which makes sense if we think of \(P_t^*\) as the \(L^2\) adjoint of \(P_t\). We can also define, as before, the generator \(\mathcal L^*\) of the semigroup \(P_t^*\), and we have
\[
P_t^*
=
e^{t\mathcal L^*}.
\]
Also,
\[
\int
(\mathcal Lf)\,d\mu
=
\int
f(\mathcal L^*\mu)\,dx.
\]
Now define the law of the Markov process as
\[
\mu_t
=
P_t^*\mu,
\]
which evolves according to
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial\mu_t}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal L^*\mu_t,\\[6pt]
\mu_0=\mu.
\end{cases}
\]
Assuming \(\mu\) and \(\mu_t\) have densities, denote them by \(\rho_0(\cdot)\) and \(\rho(\cdot,t)\).
Then
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal L^*\rho,\\[6pt]
\rho(x,0)=\rho_0(x).
\end{cases}
\]
Is the Fokker–Planck, or forward Kolmogorov, equation.
To conclude this introduction, the backward and forward Kolmogorov equations describe the evolution of the same Markov process from two complementary perspectives.
The backward Kolmogorov equation governs the evolution of an observable \(f\), as it tells us how the expected future value of \(f(X_t)\) depends on the initial state \(x\):
\[
\partial_t u=\mathcal L u.
\]
The forward Kolmogorov equation, instead, governs the evolution of the law of the process. If \(\rho(x,t)\) is the probability density of \(X_t\), then
\[
\partial_t\rho=\mathcal L^*\rho.
\]
Hence, \(\mathcal L\) propagates observables, while its adjoint \(\mathcal L^*\) propagates probability distributions.

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
A Markov process consists of three parts:

a drift;
a random part;
a jump process.

A diffusion process is a Markov process with continuous paths, hence no jumps.
In one dimension, we need the following.


For all \(\varepsilon>0\) and all \(x\),
\[
\int_{|x-y|>\varepsilon}
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
o(t-s).
\]



There exists \(b(x,s)\) such that, for all \(\varepsilon>0\) and all \(x\),
\[
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
(y-x)
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
b(x,s)(t-s)
+
o(t-s).
\]



There exists \(\Sigma(x,s)\) such that, for all \(\varepsilon>0\) and all \(x\),
\[
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
(y-x)^2
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
\Sigma(x,s)(t-s)
+
o(t-s).
\]
Assuming that the first two moments exist, we can write, even more intuitively,
\[
b(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\mathbb E
\left[
\frac{X_t-X_s}{t-s}
\mid X_s=x
\right],
\]
and
\[
\Sigma(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\mathbb E
\left[
\frac{(X_t-X_s)^2}{t-s}
\mid X_s=x
\right].
\]

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
From the definition of a diffusion process, we can derive explicit formulas for the forward and backward Kolmogorov equations.


Let
\[
u(x,s)
:=
\mathbb E[f(X_t)\mid X_s=x]
=
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s).
\]
Then \(u(x,s)\) solves the final value problem for a PDE of parabolic type:
\[
\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial s}
=
b(x,s)
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s)
\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2},
\\[8pt]
u(x,t)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
Parts of the proof are very interesting, so I recommend reading it at least once.
Proof:
The continuity assumption for the diffusion process, together with the boundedness of \(f\), implies that
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x,s)
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&\leq
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
\lVert f\rVert_{L^\infty}
\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
o(t-s).
\end{aligned}
\]
We add and subtract the final condition \(f(x)\) and use the previous calculation to obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x,s)
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
f(x)
+
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
f(x)
+
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&\qquad
+
\int_{|y-x|>\varepsilon}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
\\
&=
f(x)
+
\int_{|y-x|\leq\varepsilon}
\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)P(dy,t\mid x,s)
+
o(t-s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Now we show that \(u(s,x)\) solves the backward Kolmogorov equation. We use the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(x,\sigma)
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
f(z)P(dz,t\mid x,\sigma)
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
f(z)P(dz,t\mid y,\rho)
P(dy,\rho\mid x,\sigma)
\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
u(y,\rho)P(dy,\rho\mid x,\sigma).
\end{aligned}
\]
Where we are integrating over future paths. We use Taylor’s theorem to obtain
\[
u(z,\rho)-u(x,\rho)
=
\frac{\partial u(x,\rho)}{\partial x}(z-x)
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{\partial^2u(x,\rho)}{\partial x^2}
(z-x)^2(1+\alpha_\varepsilon),
\qquad |z-x|\leq\varepsilon,
\]
where
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\alpha_\varepsilon=0.
\]
Now we will use the last two results:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{u(x,s)-u(x,s+h)}{h}
&=
\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)u(y,s+h)
-
u(x,s+h)
\right)
\\
&=
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
\bigl(u(y,s+h)-u(x,s+h)\bigr)
\\
&=
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{|x-y|<\varepsilon}
P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
\bigl(u(y,s+h)-u(x,s+h)\bigr)
+
o(1)
\\
&=
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x,s+h)
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{|x-y|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
\\
&\qquad
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}(x,s+h)
\frac{1}{h}
\int_{|x-y|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)^2P(dy,s+h\mid x,s)
(1+\alpha_\varepsilon)
+
o(1)
\\
&=
b(x,s)
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}(x,s+h)
+
\frac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s)
\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}(x,s+h)
(1+\alpha_\varepsilon)
+
o(1).
\end{aligned}
\]
where we have used the definition of the drift and diffusion coefficients in the last step. The result follows by taking the limit \(h\to0\) and \(\varepsilon\to0\).
If \(b=b(x)\) and \(\Sigma=\Sigma(x)\), we can rewrite this as an initial value problem by letting
\[
v=u(x,t-s).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial(t-s)}
=
b(x)\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x)
\dfrac{\partial^2v}{\partial x^2},
\\[8pt]
v(x,0)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
In the time-homogeneous case, we can finally set \(s=0\) to write
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
b(x)\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x)
\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2},
\\[8pt]
u(x,0)=f(x),
\end{cases}
\]
where
\[
\mathcal L
=
b(x)\partial_x
+
\frac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x)\partial_{xx}.
\]



We have
\[
P(dy,t\mid x,s)
=
p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy.
\]
Under suitable conditions, the transition probability density is the solution to the initial value problem
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial t}
=
-\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}
\left(
b(t,y)p
\right)
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\dfrac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2}
\left(
\Sigma(t,y)p
\right),
\\[10pt]
p(y,s\mid x,s)
=
\delta(x-y).
\end{cases}
\]
The proof is less interesting than the backward case, but it is presented for completeness.
Proof:
Fix \(f(y)\in C_0^2(\mathbb{R})\). An argument similar to that used in the proof of the backward Kolmogorov equation gives
\[
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{1}{h}
\left(
\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)p(y,s+h\mid x,s)\,dy-f(x)
\right)
=
b(x,s)\frac{df}{dx}(x)
+
\frac{1}{2}\Sigma(x,s)\frac{d^2f}{dx^2}(x).
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}
f(y)\frac{\partial}{\partial t}p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(y)p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy
\\
&=
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{1}{h}
\int_{\mathbb{R}}

-

title: Diffusion Processes
text:
For a process in \(\mathbb R^d\), we define the drift and diffusion coefficients
\[
b(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\frac{1}{t-s}
\int_{|y-x|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)
P(dy,t\mid x,s),
\]
and
\[
\Sigma(x,s)
=
\lim_{t\to s}
\frac{1}{t-s}
\int_{|y-x|<\varepsilon}
(y-x)\otimes(y-x)
P(dy,t\mid x,s).
\]
As before, the generator is
\[
\mathcal L
=
b(x,s)\cdot\nabla
+
\frac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s):\nabla\nabla,
\]
where
\[

=
\sum_{i,j}
A_{ij}
\frac{\partial^2f}
{\partial x_i\partial x_j}.
\]


The backward Kolmogorov equation is
\[
\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial s}
=
b(x,s)\cdot\nabla_xu
+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\Sigma(x,s):\nabla_x\nabla_xu,
\\[10pt]
u(t,x)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]
For a time-homogeneous process, this becomes
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}
=
\mathcal Lu,
\\[6pt]
u(x,0)=f(x).
\end{cases}
\]



The forward Kolmogorov equation is
\[
\begin{cases}

=
\nabla_y\cdot
\left(

+
\dfrac{1}{2}
\nabla_y\cdot
\left(
\Sigma(t,y)p
\right)
\right),
\\[10pt]

=

\end{cases}

For a time-homogeneous process,
\[
\begin{cases}

=

\]

title: Martingales and Other Beasts
text:
Before introducing Brownian motion, it is useful to organize the main objects that appear in stochastic analysis.
A stochastic process is not merely a collection of random variables. We also care about:

how information accumulates through time;
whether the process has memory;
whether its statistical properties change through time;
whether its future values are, in a precise sense, unpredictable from current information.

These ideas lead naturally to filtrations, martingales, stationary processes, Gaussian processes, and Markov processes.



A stochastic process contains an uncountable collection of random variables, but we can probe its law through finite collections of times.
For times
\[
t_1,\ldots,t_n,
\]
consider the random vector
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n}).
\]
Its distribution is called a finite-dimensional distribution of \(X\).
The collection of all such distributions describes the joint probabilistic behaviour of the process at arbitrary finite sets of times.
This is an important distinction:
\[
\text{law of one }X_t
\]
describes the process at one time, whereas
\[
\text{finite-dimensional distributions}
\]
also describe dependence across time.
Two processes can have identical one-time distributions while having completely different dynamics.




A process is called stationary when its statistical behaviour does not change under shifts in time.
There are two important notions.


A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}\) is strictly stationary if, for every \(n\), every choice of times \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), and every time shift \(h\),
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})
\overset{d}{=}
(X_{t_1+h},\ldots,X_{t_n+h}),
\]
whenever the shifted times remain in the time domain.
Thus all finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time translation.
Strict stationarity is therefore a statement about the entire law of the process.




Suppose \(X_t\in L^2\).
The process is weakly stationary, or second-order stationary, if
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
=
\mu
\]
is independent of \(t\), and the covariance depends only on the time difference:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_s)
=
C(t-s).
\]
For a centered process,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]=0,
\]
this becomes
\[
C(t-s)
=
\mathbb{E}[X_tX_s].
\]
The function \(C\) is called the autocovariance or correlation function.
Thus weak stationarity says that the first two moments are invariant under time translation.
Strict stationarity is stronger in general:
\[
\text{strict stationarity}
+
X_t\in L^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{weak stationarity}.
\]
The converse is generally false.




These concepts should not be confused.
A process has stationary increments if the law of
\[
X_{t+h}-X_t
\]
depends only on \(h\), not on \(t\).
That is,
\[
X_{t+h}-X_t
\overset{d}{=}
X_h-X_0.
\]
A process may have stationary increments without itself being stationary.
This distinction will matter immediately when we introduce Brownian motion.





Martingales formalize the idea of a process with no predictable drift.
Let \(\{X_t\}\) be adapted to a filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_t\}\).
The process is a martingale if
\[
\mathbb{E}[|X_t|]<\infty
\]
for every \(t\), and for all \(s\leq t\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
=
X_s.
\]
This is one of the central definitions of stochastic analysis.
The interpretation is:

given all information available at time \(s\), the best prediction of the future value \(X_t\) is simply the current value \(X_s\).

A martingale is therefore a mathematical model of a fair game.



The condition
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
=
X_s
\]
does not mean that \(X_t\) is independent of the past.
Indeed, \(X_t\) generally depends strongly on \(X_s\).
The condition concerns only its conditional mean.
Equivalently,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t-X_s\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
=
0.
\]
So the future increment has zero conditional expectation.




Using the tower property,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}[X_s].
\]
Hence every martingale satisfies
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
=
\mathbb{E}[X_0].
\]
A martingale therefore has constant mean.
The converse is false: a process can have constant expectation without being a martingale.
A martingale is a conditional statement, not merely an unconditional one.




Let \(Y\in L^1\) and define
\[
M_t
=
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{F}_t].
\]
Then \(\{M_t\}\) is a martingale.
Indeed, if \(s\leq t\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[M_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{F}_t]
\mid\mathcal{F}_s
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
=
M_s.
\]
This is perhaps the cleanest interpretation of martingales:
\[
M_t
=
\text{our current best estimate of some future quantity }Y.
\]
As information grows, the estimate changes, but it remains conditionally unbiased.




A process is a submartingale if
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
\geq
X_s,
\qquad s\leq t,
\]
and a supermartingale if
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
\leq
X_s.
\]
Thus, informally,
\[
\text{submartingale}
\quad\leftrightarrow\quad
\text{non-negative expected drift},
\]
while
\[
\text{supermartingale}
\quad\leftrightarrow\quad
\text{non-positive expected drift}.
\]
Martingales are the boundary case where the conditional expected drift is zero.




If \(X_t\) is a martingale and \(\varphi\) is convex, then Jensen’s inequality for conditional expectations gives
\[
\varphi(X_t)
\]
as a submartingale, provided the relevant expectations exist.
Indeed,
\[
\mathbb{E}
[
\varphi(X_t)
\mid
\mathcal{F}_s
]
\geq
\varphi
\left(
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
\right)
=
\varphi(X_s).
\]
For example, if \(X_t\) is a martingale,
\[
X_t^2
\]
is typically a submartingale.




Martingales will become central for at least three reasons.
First, stochastic integrals of the Itô type are naturally martingales.
Second, many stochastic processes can be decomposed into
\[
\text{predictable drift}
+
\text{martingale noise}.
\]
Third, martingale arguments provide powerful tools for stopping problems, stochastic control, finance, and PDE representations.





Before defining a Gaussian process, recall that a random vector
\[
X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)
\]
is jointly Gaussian if every linear combination
\[
a_1X_1+\cdots+a_nX_n
\]
is a Gaussian random variable.
A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t\in T}\) is a Gaussian process if every finite-dimensional random vector
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})
\]
is jointly Gaussian.
Thus, a Gaussian process is not defined by requiring each \(X_t\) individually to be Gaussian. The variables must be jointly Gaussian across time.



Define the mean function
\[
m(t)
=
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
\]
and covariance function
\[
C(t,s)
=
\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_s).
\]
For any finite collection \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\),
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})
\]
has mean vector
\[
\mu_i=m(t_i)
\]
and covariance matrix
\[
K_{ij}
=
C(t_i,t_j).
\]
Since a Gaussian random vector is completely determined by its mean and covariance matrix, a Gaussian process is completely characterized by
\[
m(t)
\]
and
\[
C(t,s).
\]
This is one reason Gaussian processes are unusually tractable: infinitely many finite-dimensional distributions are encoded by only two deterministic functions.




A covariance function must satisfy
\[
C(t,s)=C(s,t)
\]
and must be non-negative definite.
For arbitrary times \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) and coefficients \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\sum_{j=1}^n
a_i a_j C(t_i,t_j)
\geq
0.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\sum_{i,j}
a_i a_j C(t_i,t_j)
=
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\sum_i a_i X_{t_i}
\right)
\geq0.
\]
Hence one cannot choose an arbitrary function \(C(t,s)\) and declare it to be a covariance kernel.




For a Gaussian process, weak stationarity is enough to imply strict stationarity.
The reason is that the finite-dimensional distributions are completely determined by their means and covariance matrices.
Hence, if
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
=
\mu
\]
and
\[
C(t,s)
=
C(t-s),
\]
then shifting all times leaves the mean vector and covariance matrix unchanged.
Therefore,
\[
\text{Gaussian + weakly stationary}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{strictly stationary}.
\]
For Gaussian processes, the two notions of stationarity therefore coincide, assuming finite second moments.




Another special feature of Gaussian systems is that zero covariance implies independence.
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are jointly Gaussian and
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0,
\]
then
\[
X\perp Y.
\]
This fact will later make Gaussian processes particularly easy to analyze through their covariance functions.





A Markov process formalizes a different idea: the future depends on the present, but not on the entire past.
Let
\[
\mathcal{F}_t^X
=
\sigma(X_s:s\leq t)
\]
be the natural filtration of \(X\).
The process is Markov if, for every \(s\leq t\) and every measurable set \(A\),
\[
\mathbb{P}
(
X_t\in A
\mid
\mathcal{F}_s^X
)
=
\mathbb{P}
(
X_t\in A
\mid
X_s
).
\]
The left-hand side conditions on the entire history
\[
\{X_r:r\leq s\},
\]
whereas the right-hand side conditions only on the current state \(X_s\).
Thus the Markov property says:

once the present state is known, the past contains no additional information useful for predicting the future.




A Markov process can have very strong temporal dependence.
The Markov property does not say
\[
X_t
\perp
X_s.
\]
Rather, it says that the present state contains all relevant information from the past.
Schematically,
\[
\text{past}
\longrightarrow
X_s
\longrightarrow
\text{future}.
\]
Once \(X_s\) is given, the earlier history becomes irrelevant for predicting the future.




A Markov process can be described through its transition probabilities
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
\mathbb{P}
(
X_t\in A
\mid
X_s=x
).
\]
If a density exists, we write
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_A
p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy,
\]
where
\[
p(y,t\mid x,s)
\]
is the transition density.
It tells us the distribution of the future state \(X_t\) given that the process is at \(x\) at time \(s\).




A Markov process is time-homogeneous if its transition probabilities depend only on the elapsed time:
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
P(A,t-s\mid x,0).
\]
We can therefore write
\[
P_\tau(x,A)
=
\mathbb{P}
(
X_{t+\tau}\in A
\mid
X_t=x
).
\]
For a time-homogeneous process, the transition law depends on
\[
\text{current state}
+
\text{time elapsed},
\]
but not on the absolute calendar time.




Suppose
\[
s<u<t.
\]
A Markov process can travel from \(x\) at time \(s\) to a set \(A\) at time \(t\) by passing through some intermediate state \(y\) at time \(u\).
Summing over all possible intermediate states gives the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_E
P(A,t\mid y,u)
P(dy,u\mid x,s).
\]
If transition densities exist,
\[
p(z,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_E
p(z,t\mid y,u)
p(y,u\mid x,s)\,dy.
\]
This is the probabilistic analogue of a composition law.
For a time-homogeneous Markov process,
\[
P_{t+s}
=
P_tP_s.
\]
This semigroup structure will later lead directly to generators and Kolmogorov equations.




Whether a model is Markov depends crucially on the choice of state variables.
A process may fail to be Markov because its current value does not contain enough information about its future evolution.
Sometimes this can be fixed by enlarging the state.
For example, suppose position satisfies
\[
X_t
=
X_0
+
\int_0^t V_s\,ds.
\]
Knowing \(X_t\) alone may not be sufficient to predict the future, because the current velocity \(V_t\) also matters.
But the enlarged state
\[
(X_t,V_t)
\]
may be Markov.
This is an important modelling principle:

choose the state so that the present contains all information required to determine future probabilities.

Markovianity is therefore not merely a mathematical property. It is also a statement about whether we have chosen an adequate state representation.





The properties introduced above describe different aspects of a stochastic process.
Stationarity concerns invariance through time:
\[
\text{do the statistics change when time is shifted?}
\]
Gaussianity concerns the shape of finite-dimensional distributions:
\[
\text{are all finite collections jointly Gaussian?}
\]
The Markov property concerns memory:
\[
\text{is the present state sufficient to predict the future?}
\]
The martingale property concerns conditional drift:
\[
\text{is the current value already the best prediction of the future value?}
\]
These properties are logically distinct.
A process can be Markov but not stationary.
A process can be stationary but not Markov.
A process can be Gaussian but not Markov.
A process can be Markov but not a martingale.
The interesting stochastic processes we encounter later arise from particular combinations of these properties.
Brownian motion, for example, will turn out to be a continuous Gaussian Markov process with stationary independent increments and a martingale structure.
At that point, rather than memorizing a list of mysterious Brownian-motion properties, we will already know what each of those words means.

as a submartingale, provided the relevant expectations exist.
Indeed,
\[
\mathbb{E}
[
\varphi(X_t)
\mid
\mathcal{F}_s
]
\geq
\varphi
\left(
\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]
\right)
=
\varphi(X_s).
\]
For example, if \(X_t\) is a martingale,
\[
X_t^2
\]
is typically a submartingale.




Martingales will become central for at least three reasons.
First, stochastic integrals of the Itô type are naturally martingales.
Second, many stochastic processes can be decomposed into
\[
\text{predictable drift}
+
\text{martingale noise}.
\]
Third, martingale arguments provide powerful tools for stopping problems, stochastic control, finance, and PDE representations.

title: Martingales and Other Beasts
text:
Before defining a Gaussian process, recall that a random vector
\[
X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)
\]
is jointly Gaussian if every linear combination
\[
a_1X_1+\cdots+a_nX_n
\]
is a Gaussian random variable.
A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}_{t\in T}\) is a Gaussian process if every finite-dimensional random vector
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})
\]
is jointly Gaussian.
Thus, a Gaussian process is not defined by requiring each \(X_t\) individually to be Gaussian. The variables must be jointly Gaussian across time.



Define the mean function
\[
m(t)
=
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
\]
and covariance function
\[
C(t,s)
=
\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_s).
\]
For any finite collection \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\),
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})
\]
has mean vector
\[
\mu_i=m(t_i)
\]
and covariance matrix
\[
K_{ij}
=
C(t_i,t_j).
\]
Since a Gaussian random vector is completely determined by its mean and covariance matrix, a Gaussian process is completely characterized by
\[
m(t)
\]
and
\[
C(t,s).
\]
This is one reason Gaussian processes are unusually tractable: infinitely many finite-dimensional distributions are encoded by only two deterministic functions.




A covariance function must satisfy
\[
C(t,s)=C(s,t)
\]
and must be non-negative definite.
For arbitrary times \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) and coefficients \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n
\sum_{j=1}^n
a_i a_j C(t_i,t_j)
\geq
0.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\sum_{i,j}
a_i a_j C(t_i,t_j)
=
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\sum_i a_i X_{t_i}
\right)
\geq0.
\]
Hence one cannot choose an arbitrary function \(C(t,s)\) and declare it to be a covariance kernel.




For a Gaussian process, weak stationarity is enough to imply strict stationarity.
The reason is that the finite-dimensional distributions are completely determined by their means and covariance matrices.
Hence, if
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
=
\mu
\]
and
\[
C(t,s)
=
C(t-s),
\]
then shifting all times leaves the mean vector and covariance matrix unchanged.
Therefore,
\[
\text{Gaussian + weakly stationary}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{strictly stationary}.
\]
For Gaussian processes, the two notions of stationarity therefore coincide, assuming finite second moments.




Another special feature of Gaussian systems is that zero covariance implies independence.
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are jointly Gaussian and
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0,
\]
then
\[
X\perp Y.
\]
This fact will later make Gaussian processes particularly easy to analyze through their covariance functions.

title: Martingales and Other Beasts
text:
A Markov process formalizes a different idea: the future depends on the present, but not on the entire past.
Let
\[
\mathcal{F}_t^X
=
\sigma(X_s:s\leq t)
\]
be the natural filtration of \(X\).
The process is Markov if, for every \(s\leq t\) and every measurable set \(A\),
\[
\mathbb{P}
(
X_t\in A
\mid
\mathcal{F}_s^X
)
=
\mathbb{P}
(
X_t\in A
\mid
X_s
).
\]
The left-hand side conditions on the entire history
\[
\{X_r:r\leq s\},
\]
whereas the right-hand side conditions only on the current state \(X_s\).
Thus the Markov property says:

once the present state is known, the past contains no additional information useful for predicting the future.




A Markov process can have very strong temporal dependence.
The Markov property does not say
\[
X_t
\perp
X_s.
\]
Rather, it says that the present state contains all relevant information from the past.
Schematically,
\[
\text{past}
\longrightarrow
X_s
\longrightarrow
\text{future}.
\]
Once \(X_s\) is given, the earlier history becomes irrelevant for predicting the future.




A Markov process can be described through its transition probabilities
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
\mathbb{P}
(
X_t\in A
\mid
X_s=x
).
\]
If a density exists, we write
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_A
p(y,t\mid x,s)\,dy,
\]
where
\[
p(y,t\mid x,s)
\]
is the transition density.
It tells us the distribution of the future state \(X_t\) given that the process is at \(x\) at time \(s\).




A Markov process is time-homogeneous if its transition probabilities depend only on the elapsed time:
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
P(A,t-s\mid x,0).
\]
We can therefore write
\[
P_\tau(x,A)
=
\mathbb{P}
(
X_{t+\tau}\in A
\mid
X_t=x
).
\]
For a time-homogeneous process, the transition law depends on
\[
\text{current state}
+
\text{time elapsed},
\]
but not on the absolute calendar time.




Suppose
\[
s<u<t.
\]
A Markov process can travel from \(x\) at time \(s\) to a set \(A\) at time \(t\) by passing through some intermediate state \(y\) at time \(u\).
Summing over all possible intermediate states gives the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation
\[
P(A,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_E
P(A,t\mid y,u)
P(dy,u\mid x,s).
\]
If transition densities exist,
\[
p(z,t\mid x,s)
=
\int_E
p(z,t\mid y,u)
p(y,u\mid x,s)\,dy.
\]
This is the probabilistic analogue of a composition law.
For a time-homogeneous Markov process,
\[
P_{t+s}
=
P_tP_s.
\]
This semigroup structure will later lead directly to generators and Kolmogorov equations.




Whether a model is Markov depends crucially on the choice of state variables.
A process may fail to be Markov because its current value does not contain enough information about its future evolution.
Sometimes this can be fixed by enlarging the state.
For example, suppose position satisfies
\[
X_t
=
X_0
+
\int_0^t V_s\,ds.
\]
Knowing \(X_t\) alone may not be sufficient to predict the future, because the current velocity \(V_t\) also matters.
But the enlarged state
\[
(X_t,V_t)
\]
may be Markov.
This is an important modelling principle:

choose the state so that the present contains all information required to determine future probabilities.

Markovianity is therefore not merely a mathematical property. It is also a statement about whether we have chosen an adequate state representation.

title: Martingales and Other Beasts
text:
The properties introduced above describe different aspects of a stochastic process.
Stationarity concerns invariance through time:
\[
\text{do the statistics change when time is shifted?}
\]
Gaussianity concerns the shape of finite-dimensional distributions:
\[
\text{are all finite collections jointly Gaussian?}
\]
The Markov property concerns memory:
\[
\text{is the present state sufficient to predict the future?}
\]
The martingale property concerns conditional drift:
\[
\text{is the current value already the best prediction of the future value?}
\]
These properties are logically distinct.
A process can be Markov but not stationary.
A process can be stationary but not Markov.
A process can be Gaussian but not Markov.
A process can be Markov but not a martingale.
The interesting stochastic processes we encounter later arise from particular combinations of these properties.
Brownian motion, for example, will turn out to be a continuous Gaussian Markov process with stationary independent increments and a martingale structure.
At that point, rather than memorizing a list of mysterious Brownian-motion properties, we will already know what each of those words means.

title: Brownian motion: definition and properties
text:
I choose to open this series of notes with a discussion of Brownian motion, arguably the most popular stochastic process in the theory of SDE. Prerequisites for this part are a basic knowledge of probability and measure theory.


A stochastic process is a family of random variables
\[
X=\{X_t\}_{t\in T}
\]
defined on the same probability space
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}),
\]
with values in some state space \(E\).
Usually,
\[
T=[0,\infty)
\]
and
\[
E=\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
The process can equivalently be viewed as a function of two variables,
\[
X:T\times\Omega\to E,
\]
with
\[
X(t,\omega)=X_t(\omega).
\]
There are two complementary ways to look at it.
For fixed \(t\),
\[
\omega\mapsto X_t(\omega)
\]
is a random variable.
For fixed \(\omega\),
\[
t\mapsto X_t(\omega)
\]
is a function of time, called a sample path, trajectory, or realization of the process.



A process is called stationary when its statistical behaviour does not change under shifts in time.
There are two important notions.


A stochastic process \(\{X_t\}\) is strictly stationary if, for every \(n\), every choice of times \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), and every time shift \(h\),
\[
(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})
\overset{d}{=}
(X_{t_1+h},\ldots,X_{t_n+h}),
\]
whenever the shifted times remain in the time domain.
Thus all finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under time translation.
Strict stationarity is therefore a statement about the entire law of the process.




Suppose \(X_t\in L^2\).
The process is weakly stationary, or second-order stationary, if
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]
=
\mu
\]
is independent of \(t\), and the covariance depends only on the time difference:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_s)
=
C(t-s).
\]
For a centered process,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X_t]=0,
\]
this becomes
\[
C(t-s)
=
\mathbb{E}[X_tX_s].
\]
The function \(C\) is called the autocovariance or correlation function.
Thus weak stationarity says that the first two moments are invariant under time translation.
Strict stationarity is stronger in general:
\[
\text{strict stationarity}
+
X_t\in L^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{weak stationarity}.
\]
The converse is generally false.



\(X_t\) has independent increments if, for all
\[
t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n,
\]
the random variables
\[
X_{t_1}-X_{t_0}, \quad
X_{t_2}-X_{t_1}, \quad \ldots
\]
are independent.
If, for all \(t_1,t_2,s\in T\) and \(B\subset\mathbb R\),
\[
\mathbb P(X_{t_1+s}-X_{t_1}\in B)
=
\mathbb P(X_{t_2+s}-X_{t_2}\in B),
\]
then \(X_t\) has stationary independent increments.




A Brownian motion
\[
W(t):\mathbb R^+\to\mathbb R
\]
is a real-valued stochastic process with a.s. continuous paths such that
\[
W(0)=0,
\]
it has independent increments, and, for all \(t>s\geq 0\),
\[
W(t)-W(s)
\]
has a Gaussian distribution with mean \(0\) and variance \(t-s\):
\[
W(t)-W(s)\sim\mathcal N(0,t-s).
\]
The density of the random variable \(W(t)-W(s)\) is
\[
g(x;t,s)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(t-s)}}
\exp\left(
-\frac{x^2}{2(t-s)}
\right).
\]
Although Brownian motion has stationary increments, it is not a stationary process. The probability density of the one-dimensional Brownian motion is
\[
g(x,t)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}
\exp\left(
-\frac{x^2}{2t}
\right).
\]
Similarly, a \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion
\[
W(t):\mathbb R^+\to\mathbb R^d
\]
is a vector of \(d\) independent Brownian motions,
\[
W(t)
=
\left(
W_1(t),\ldots,W_d(t)
\right).
\]
The density of the Gaussian random variable \(W(t)-W(s)\) is
\[
g(x;t,s)
=
\frac{1}{[2\pi(t-s)]^{d/2}}
\exp\left(
-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2(t-s)}
\right).
\]
For \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion,
\[
\mathbb E[W(t)] = 0,
\qquad \forall t\geq 0,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
(W(t)-W(s))
\otimes
(W(t)-W(s))
\right]
=
(t-s)I.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
W(t)\otimes W(s)
\right]
=
\min(t,s)I.
\]



The following properties will be central to the development of stochastic calculus. I choose to present them in a non-technical way, using heuristic arguments rather than proofs.


Brownian paths are almost surely locally Hölder continuous with any exponent
\[
\alpha \in \left(0,\frac12\right).
\]
That is, for every \(T>0\) and \(\alpha<1/2\), there exists an a.s. finite random constant \(C\) such that
\[
|W_t-W_s|
\leq C|t-s|^\alpha,
\qquad s,t\in[0,T].
\]



For a partition
\[
\Pi=\{0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=t\},
\]
define
\[
\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k},
\qquad
\Delta t_k=t_{k+1}-t_k,
\]
Since (remember that \(\Delta W_k\sim\mathcal N(0,\Delta t_k)\))
\[
\mathbb E[(\Delta W_k)^2]=\Delta t_k,
\qquad
\mathbb E[(\Delta W_k)^4]=3(\Delta t_k)^2,
\]
we have
\[
\mathbb E[\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2]
=
\sum_{t_k<t}\Delta t_k
=
t.
\]
Moreover, by independence of the increments,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2-t)^2]
&=
\sum_{t_k<t}
\mathbb E
\left[
\left((\Delta W_k)^2-\Delta t_k\right)^2
\right]
\\
&=
\sum_{t_k<t}
\left(
3(\Delta t_k)^2-(\Delta t_k)^2
\right)
\\
&=
2\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta t_k)^2
\longrightarrow 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2.
=
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2
\longrightarrow t
\qquad\text{in }L^2.
\]
Now suppose, by contradiction, that a Brownian path has bounded variation on \([0,t]\). Then
\[
V_t(W)
=
\sup_{\Pi}
\sum_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|
<\infty,
\]
so, for every partition \(\Pi\),
\[
\sum_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|
\leq V_t(W).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2
&=
\sum_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|\,|\Delta W_k|
\\
&\leq
\max_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|
\sum_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|
\\
&\leq
\max_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|\,V_t(W).
\end{aligned}
\]
As \(|\Pi|\to0\), continuity of the Brownian path on the compact interval \([0,t]\) implies uniform continuity, and therefore
\[
\max_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Since \(V_t(W)<\infty\) by assumption,
\[
0
\leq
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2
\leq
\max_{t_k<t}|\Delta W_k|\,V_t(W)
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Hence a continuous path of bounded variation must have zero quadratic variation:
\[
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
But for Brownian motion we have just shown that
\[
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2\longrightarrow t.
\]
For \(t>0\) this is a contradiction. Therefore
\[
V_t(W)
=
\sup_{\Pi}
\sum_{t_k<t}|W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}|
=
\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]



Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable.
This should not be surprising: Brownian motion is continuous, but its paths have infinite variation on every non-trivial time interval.



We have just shown that, in \(L^2\),
\[
\sum_{t_k<t}(\Delta W_k)^2
\longrightarrow t.
\]
This is conventionally written
\[
(dW_t)^2=dt
\]
or, informally over a small increment,
\[
(\Delta W)^2\sim\Delta t.
\]
Since the second-order term contributes at the same order as an ordinary time increment it cannot be discarded when Taylor-expanding functions of Brownian motion.



For a Brownian increment,
\[
\Delta W
=
W_{t+\Delta t}-W_t
\sim
\mathcal N(0,\Delta t).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\Delta W=\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z,
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\]
Thus a Brownian increment is of order \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\). Consequently,
\[
(\Delta W)^2
=
\Delta t\,Z^2,
\]
is of order \(\Delta t\), while
\[
\Delta W\,\Delta t
=
(\Delta t)^{3/2}Z
\]
and
\[
(\Delta t)^2
\]
are of higher order.
As before we could show that, in \(L^2\),
\[
\sum_k\Delta W_k\,\Delta t_k
\longrightarrow 0,
\qquad
\sum_k(\Delta t_k)^2
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
which gives
\[
dW_t\,dt=0,
\qquad
(dt)^2=0.
\]



Let \(W_t\) be a one-dimensional Brownian motion and let \(c>0\). Define
\[
\frac{1}{c}W_{c^2t}.
\]
is again a Brownian motion.
Equivalently, setting \(a=c^2\),
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt a}W_{at}
\overset{d}{=}W_t.
\]
This is the Brownian scaling property.



For every \(c>0\), the process
\[
X_t=W_{c+t}-W_c
\]
is a Brownian motion independent of
\[
\{W_u:u\in[0,c]\}.
\]



Let
\[
X_t=W_{1-t}-W_1,
\qquad t\in[0,1].
\]
Then
\[
X_t\overset{d}{=}W_t.
\]



Define
\[
X_0=0,
\qquad
X_t=tW_{1/t},
\quad t>0.
\]
Then
\[
X_t\overset{d}{=}W_t.
\]

title: Probability Preliminaries
text:
Before studying stochastic processes, it is useful to understand the basic objects on which probability theory is built.
The definitions can initially look unnecessarily abstract. They are not.
The main purpose of this section is to understand this construction and become familiar with the language that will be used later.





A random experiment may have many possible outcomes. We collect all of them in a set called the sample space
\[
\Omega.
\]
An individual outcome is denoted by \(\omega\in\Omega\).
For a coin toss,
\[
\Omega=\{H,T\}.
\]
For a stochastic trajectory, however, an outcome \(\omega\) may eventually represent an entire path. Thus \(\Omega\) should be thought of abstractly as the universe containing all possible realizations of the random system.
Usually we are not interested in individual outcomes, but in statements about them. Such statements correspond to subsets of \(\Omega\).
For example,
\[
A=\{\omega:\text{the outcome satisfies some property}\}
\]
is called an event.
We would like to assign probabilities to events.
The first temptation would therefore be to assign probabilities to every subset of \(\Omega\). For finite spaces this works perfectly well. For sufficiently complicated infinite spaces, however, it is impossible to construct a useful probability measure on every possible subset.
We therefore specify which subsets are admissible events.





Suppose \(A\) is an event. Then we naturally also want
\[
A^c
\]
to be an event.
Likewise, if \(A\) and \(B\) are events, then statements such as
\[
A\cup B
\]
and
\[
A\cap B
\]
should also be events.
This motivates the algebraic structure imposed on collections of events.
A collection \(\mathcal{F}\) of subsets of \(\Omega\) is called a field if
\[
\emptyset\in\mathcal{F},
\]
\[
A\in\mathcal{F}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A^c\in\mathcal{F},
\]
and
\[
A,B\in\mathcal{F}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A\cup B\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
Consequently, a field is closed under finite unions and finite intersections.
In probability we regularly encounter limits involving infinitely many events. Finite closure is therefore not enough.
A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) strengthens the previous requirement by demanding closure under countable unions:
\[
A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\mathcal{F}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
Together with closure under complements, this also implies
\[
\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty A_n\in\mathcal{F}.
\]
So a \(\sigma\)-algebra is simply a collection of events stable under the logical operations that probability theory needs.


Often we begin with a natural collection of sets \(\mathcal{C}\) but it is not itself a \(\sigma\)-algebra.
We then define
\[
\sigma(\mathcal{C})
\]
to be the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra containing \(\mathcal{C}\).
This is an important recurring construction: rather than arbitrarily choosing a huge collection of measurable sets, we start from the sets that matter and add exactly what is required for the \(\sigma\)-algebra axioms to hold.





Suppose our state space is \(\mathbb{R}\).
Intervals such as
\[
(a,b),
\qquad
(-\infty,x],
\]
are clearly sets to which we would like to assign probabilities.
Instead of choosing all subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\), we begin with its open sets and generate a \(\sigma\)-algebra from them:
\[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})
=
\sigma(\text{open subsets of }\mathbb{R}).
\]
This is called the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra.
More generally,
\[
\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)
\]
is the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
The Borel sets are therefore the sets naturally compatible with the topology of the state space.




A set together with a \(\sigma\)-algebra,
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal{F}),
\]
is called a measurable space.
At this stage there is still no probability. We have only specified which questions about \(\omega\) we are allowed to ask.
We now attach probabilities to those events.
A probability measure is a function
\[
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal{F}\to[0,1]
\]
such that
\[
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\emptyset)=0,
\]
and for pairwise disjoint events \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\),
\[
\mathbb{P}
\left(
\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n
\right)
=
\sum_{n=1}^\infty
\mathbb{P}(A_n).
\]
The triple
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})
\]
is called a probability space.
The three objects play distinct roles:

\(\Omega\) describes what can happen;
\(\mathcal{F}\) describes which events we can distinguish;
\(\mathbb{P}\) assigns probabilities to those events.





A random variable is not itself a random outcome. It is a function applied to the outcome.
Let
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal{F})
\]
be our underlying measurable space and let \((E,\mathcal{G})\) be another measurable space.
A random variable is a measurable function
\[
X:\Omega\to E.
\]
The word measurable means that
\[
X^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal{F}
\]
for every \(A\in\mathcal{G}\).
Why is this condition necessary?
Suppose we want to ask
\[
\mathbb{P}(X\in A).
\]
The probability measure \(\mathbb{P}\) acts on subsets of \(\Omega\), not on subsets of \(E\).
But
\[
X\in A
\]
really means
\[
\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in A\}
=
X^{-1}(A).
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb{P}(X\in A)
=
\mathbb{P}\left(X^{-1}(A)\right).
\]
For this expression to make sense, \(X^{-1}(A)\) must belong to \(\mathcal{F}\).
That is precisely what measurability guarantees.
For a real-valued random variable,
\[
X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R},
\]
we normally take \(\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).

Once a random variable
\[
X:\Omega\to E
\]
has been defined, it transfers the probability measure \(\mathbb{P}\) from \(\Omega\) to \(E\).
Define
\[
\mu_X(A)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\in A)
=
\mathbb{P}(X^{-1}(A)).
\]
The measure \(\mu_X\) is called the law or distribution of \(X\).
Schematically,
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})
\xrightarrow{\quad X\quad}
(E,\mathcal{G},\mu_X).
\]
This induced measure is also called the pushforward measure of \(\mathbb{P}\) through \(X\):
\[
\mu_X=X_\#\mathbb{P}.
\]
This distinction is useful:

\(\mathbb{P}\) describes randomness on the underlying sample space;
\(\mu_X\) describes the resulting distribution of the observable \(X\).

Two completely different probability spaces can therefore produce random variables with exactly the same law.
For \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\), the cumulative distribution function is
\[
F_X(x)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\leq x).
\]




Expectation is simply integration with respect to probability.
For an integrable random variable \(X\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=
\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,d\mathbb{P}(\omega).
\]
But since \(X\) induces its own probability measure \(\mu_X\), the same quantity can be computed directly on the state space:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=
\int_E x\,\mu_X(dx).
\]
More generally,
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(X)]
=
\int_\Omega f(X(\omega))\,d\mathbb{P}(\omega)
=
\int_E f(x)\,\mu_X(dx).
\]
If \(X\) admits a probability density \(p_X\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(X)]
=
\int_E f(x)p_X(x)\,dx.
\]
This is useful conceptually: once the law of \(X\) is known, expectations involving only \(X\) can be computed without referring explicitly to the original sample space \(\Omega\).




A random variable is also a measurable function, so we can classify random variables according to their integrability.
For \(1\leq p<\infty\), define
\[
L^p(\Omega)
=
\left\{
X:
\mathbb{E}[|X|^p]<\infty
\right\}.
\]
The associated norm is
\[
\|X\|_{L^p}
=
\left(
\mathbb{E}[|X|^p]
\right)^{1/p}.
\]
Thus
\[
X\in L^1
\]
means that \(X\) has a finite absolute expectation, while
\[
X\in L^2
\]
means that \(X\) has a finite second moment.
The space \(L^2\) is particularly important because it is a Hilbert space with inner product
\[
\langle X,Y\rangle_{L^2}
=
\mathbb{E}[XY].
\]
This geometric interpretation will appear repeatedly later.
As usual in measure theory, two random variables that differ only on a set of probability zero are identified as the same element of \(L^p\).
This is why statements in probability are so often made almost surely.
A property holds almost surely if the set on which it fails has probability zero.




Expectation describes the average behaviour of one variable. Covariance describes how two variables move together.
For \(X,Y\in L^2\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
(X-\mathbb{E}[X])
(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])
\right].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
=
\mathbb{E}[XY]
-
\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].
\]
The variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)
=
\operatorname{Cov}(X,X).
\]
The normalized version is the correlation coefficient
\[
\rho(X,Y)
=
\frac{
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)
}{
\sqrt{
\operatorname{Var}(X)
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
}
}.
\]
If
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0,
\]
we say that \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated.
This only says that there is no linear dependence detectable through covariance. It does not, in general, imply independence.




Two random variables are independent when knowing one gives no probabilistic information about the other.
Formally, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if
\[
\mathbb{P}(X\in A,Y\in B)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\in A)
\mathbb{P}(Y\in B)
\]
for every measurable \(A\) and \(B\).
Equivalently, their joint law factorizes:
\[
\mu_{X,Y}
=
\mu_X\otimes\mu_Y.
\]
If densities exist,
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)
=
p_X(x)p_Y(y).
\]
Independence implies, whenever the relevant expectations exist,
\[
\mathbb{E}[XY]
=
\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y],
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.
\]
The reverse implication is generally false.
The distinction is important:
\[
\text{independence}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{uncorrelated},
\]
but not conversely.




Suppose we do not know the entire outcome \(\omega\), but only some information about it.
Mathematically, information is represented by a sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra
\[
\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}.
\]
A smaller \(\sigma\)-algebra contains fewer distinguishable events and therefore represents less information.
If \(X\in L^1\), the conditional expectation
\[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
\]
is a \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variable satisfying
\[
\int_G
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
\,d\mathbb{P}
=
\int_G
X\,d\mathbb{P}
\]
for every \(G\in\mathcal{G}\).
The important point is that
\[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
\]
is itself a random variable.
It depends on \(\omega\), but it is allowed to depend only on the information contained in \(\mathcal{G}\).
In this sense, conditional expectation replaces \(X\) with the best summary of \(X\) that can be constructed using the available information.
For \(X\in L^2\), this interpretation becomes geometric: \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]\) is the orthogonal projection of \(X\) onto the subspace of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable random variables in \(L^2\).


Conditional expectation is linear:
\[
\mathbb{E}
[
aX+bY
\mid\mathcal{G}
]
=
a\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
+
b\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}].
\]
If \(X\) is already \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, then no information has been lost:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
=
X.
\]
If \(X\) is independent of \(\mathcal{G}\), then \(\mathcal{G}\) tells us nothing about \(X\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
=
\mathbb{E}[X].
\]
If \(Y\) is \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable, then
\[
\mathbb{E}[YX\mid\mathcal{G}]
=
Y\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}].
\]
If
\[
\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F},
\]
then the tower property gives
\[
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
\mid\mathcal{H}
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{H}].
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}[X].
\]
Conditional probabilities are particular conditional expectations:
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid\mathcal{G})
=
\mathbb{E}
[
\mathbf{1}_A
\mid\mathcal{G}
].
\]
